terms.title: Cosine similarity
terms.summary: Cosine similarity measures how much two vectors point in the same direction — in other words, how much two texts resemble each other.
terms.where: You'll see it in vector databases, embeddings, recommendation engines, and RAG result rankings.

terms.title: HNSW
terms.summary: HNSW is a type of index that speeds up finding nearby vectors without comparing every document one by one.
terms.where: You run into it in Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector, vector-mode Elasticsearch, and high-volume vector databases.

terms.title: Metadata filter
terms.summary: A metadata filter narrows the search to certain documents based on their source, date, client, language, type, or status.
terms.where: You run into it in serious RAG systems, when the agent should only search within the right document space.

terms.title: Vector namespace
terms.summary: A vector namespace separates sets of embeddings so you don't mix up clients, projects, languages, or environments.
terms.where: You'll run into it in Pinecone, multi-tenant vector databases, staging/prod testing, and walled-off document assistants.

terms.title: Upsert
terms.summary: An upsert creates a record if it doesn't exist, or updates it if it already does.
terms.where: You'll see it in Supabase, vector databases, document syncs, and pipelines that re-index content.

terms.title: Incremental indexing
terms.summary: Incremental indexing adds or updates only the documents that changed, instead of rebuilding the whole database.
terms.where: You'll run into it in living knowledge bases, Drive, Notion, SharePoint, websites, and production RAG.

terms.title: Chunk overlap
terms.summary: Chunk overlap keeps a small shared zone between two pieces of a document so an idea isn't cut off in the wrong place.
terms.where: You'll see it in RAG pipelines, LangChain loaders, LlamaIndex, and document-chunking settings.

terms.title: Parent document retriever
terms.summary: A parent document retriever searches within small chunks, then returns a wider passage to keep the context.
terms.where: You run into it in LangChain, documentation assistants, and RAG systems that need to avoid answers chopped up too finely.

terms.title: Contextual compression
terms.summary: Contextual compression trims the retrieved passages down to only the pieces useful to the question.
terms.where: You see it in RAG setups that want to save tokens, cut noise, and sharpen answer accuracy.

terms.title: Multi-query retrieval
terms.summary: Multi-query retrieval rephrases one question into several searches to find more relevant passages.
terms.where: You run into it in LangChain, research assistants, agentic RAG, and ambiguous questions where a single query misses documents.

terms.title: MMR
terms.summary: MMR picks results that are both relevant and different from each other, so you don't get ten near-identical passages.
terms.where: You see it in retrievers, vector databases, document search engines, and RAG systems that need diverse sources.

terms.title: RRF
terms.summary: RRF merges several search rankings to produce a more robust final list.
terms.where: You run into it in hybrid search, when a system combines BM25, vectors, reranking, or several engines.

terms.title: Cross-encoder
terms.summary: A cross-encoder compares a question and a passage directly to judge their relevance more precisely than a plain vector score.
terms.where: You'll see it in rerankers, advanced RAG engines, and systems where ranking quality matters more than raw speed.

terms.title: OCR
terms.summary: OCR turns the text inside an image or scan into text a machine can read.
terms.where: You run into it with scanned invoices, image PDFs, ID documents, paper contracts, and Document AI workflows.

terms.title: Document provenance
terms.summary: Document provenance tells you where a piece of information comes from: file, page, date, author, passage, or source system.
terms.where: You see it in RAG with citations, audits, legal workflows, compliance, and assistants that have to back up their answers.

terms.title: Faithfulness
terms.summary: Faithfulness measures whether an answer stays true to the sources it was given, instead of adding claims that aren't there.
terms.where: You'll run into it in RAG evaluations, Ragas, quality dashboards, and document-assistant tests.

terms.title: Context precision
terms.summary: Context precision measures whether the passages handed to the model are actually useful for answering the question.
terms.where: You see it in RAG testing, when you want to cut noise and check that the retriever surfaces the right documents.

terms.title: Context recall
terms.summary: Context recall measures whether the system actually retrieved all the passages needed to answer correctly.
terms.where: You'll run into it in RAG evaluations, especially when an answer needs several sources or several pieces of one file.

terms.title: Golden dataset
terms.summary: A golden dataset is a set of validated examples used as a benchmark to test AI prompts, models, or workflows.
terms.where: You see it when a team wants to compare two prompts, check for a regression, or measure an agent's quality before production.

terms.title: Zap
terms.summary: A Zap is a Zapier automation that links a trigger to one or more actions.
terms.where: You run into it when a form creates a row, sends an email, adds a lead, or notifies a team automatically.

terms.title: Make scenario
terms.summary: A Make scenario is a visual workflow that connects modules to move and transform data.
terms.where: You see it in Make with HTTP modules, routers, filters, Google Sheets, Gmail, Supabase, or OpenAI.

terms.title: Make router
terms.summary: A Make router splits a scenario into several branches based on conditions.
terms.where: You'll run into it when an automation needs to treat a hot lead, an error, an existing customer, or a new contact differently.

terms.title: Iterator
terms.summary: An iterator takes a list and turns it into items processed one by one.
terms.where: You'll see it in Make, n8n, and automations that loop over rows, attachments, products, emails, or API results.

terms.title: Aggregator
terms.summary: An aggregator groups several items processed separately back into a final list, report, or batch.
terms.where: You'll run into it after an iterator, when you need to gather results before sending an email, creating a file, or calling an API.

terms.title: Data mapping
terms.summary: Data mapping is about connecting a field from one tool to the right field in another.
terms.where: You run into it in n8n, Make, Zapier, forms, CRMs, and workflows that move a first name, email, status, or amount between services.

terms.title: Run / Execution
terms.summary: A run, or an execution, is one complete run of a workflow with its inputs, outputs, errors, and processing time.
terms.where: You'll run into it in n8n, Make, Zapier, GitHub Actions, Vercel logs, and automation dashboards.

terms.title: MCP elicitation
terms.summary: MCP elicitation lets an MCP server ask the user for a piece of information through the client.
terms.where: You'll run into it when a connected tool needs to ask for a detail, an approval, or a sensitive piece of data before moving on.

terms.title: MCP roots
terms.summary: MCP roots tell an MCP server which folders or spaces it's allowed to access.
terms.where: You'll see them in file connectors, local projects, code MCP servers, and settings that fence off the scope of access.

terms.title: MCP resource template
terms.summary: An MCP resource template describes a parameterized resource that the agent can open using a variable.
terms.where: You'll run into it when a server exposes files, tickets, tables, or pages through a dynamic address.

terms.title: MCP tasks
terms.summary: MCP tasks represent long-running operations that the client can track or resume later.
terms.where: You see them in MCP tools that launch a search, a document process, or an action that doesn't answer instantly.

terms.title: Token passthrough
terms.summary: Token passthrough means relaying a user's token to another service instead of handling a proper authorization of its own.
terms.where: You see it in MCP and OAuth discussions, when a connected server risks abusing a user's access.

terms.title: Progressive tool discovery
terms.summary: Progressive tool discovery loads only the tools that are useful, instead of handing everything to the model from the start.
terms.where: You run into it in agents with lots of MCP servers, tool catalogs, or possible actions.

terms.title: Agent credential model
terms.summary: The agent credential model defines whether the agent acts with its own access or the user's.
terms.where: You'll run into it the moment an agent can read data, publish, send an email, or change a connected tool.

terms.title: Planner / executor
terms.summary: Planner / executor splits the agent that builds the plan from the one that runs the steps.
terms.where: You see it in code, research, or support agents that need to think before they act.

terms.title: Evaluator-optimizer
terms.summary: Evaluator-optimizer is a loop where an output is produced, evaluated, then improved.
terms.where: You'll see it in agents that review their own work, compare several answers, or fix a generation before delivering it.

terms.title: Agent graph
terms.summary: An agent graph represents an agentic workflow as nodes, state, and transitions.
terms.where: You'll run into it in LangGraph, complex agents, and workflows that aren't just a straight line of steps.

terms.title: Integrated embedding
terms.summary: An integrated embedding is generated directly by the database or search service at index or query time.
terms.where: You see it in vector databases that simplify RAG pipelines by sparing you from managing the embedding model yourself.

terms.title: Payload index
terms.summary: A payload index speeds up filters on the fields attached to your vectors.
terms.where: You'll run into it in Qdrant, Weaviate, or RAG setups that filter by client, date, language, source, or status.

terms.title: Multivector
terms.summary: A multivector represents a single document with several vectors rather than just one.
terms.where: You run into it in high-precision search engines, ColBERT, late interaction, and multimodal RAG.

terms.title: Late interaction
terms.summary: Late interaction compares a question's and a document's vectors more finely after a first round of selection.
terms.where: You run into it in retrieval systems that want more precision than a single global vector score.

terms.title: IVFFlat
terms.summary: IVFFlat is a vector index that speeds up search by grouping vectors into lists.
terms.where: You'll see it in pgvector and Postgres when a vector database needs to stay fast on larger amounts of data.

terms.title: LangChain text splitter
terms.summary: A LangChain text splitter cuts documents into chunks a RAG system can actually use.
terms.where: You'll run into it in LangChain tutorials, document ingestion, chunking, and assistants that read PDFs.

terms.title: VectorStoreIndex
terms.summary: VectorStoreIndex is the LlamaIndex index that turns documents into a queryable vector search.
terms.where: You see it in LlamaIndex, RAG prototypes, document assistants, and pipelines that connect documents to a vector database.

terms.title: Ingestion pipeline
terms.summary: An ingestion pipeline chains chunking, metadata extraction, embeddings, and storage.
terms.where: You run into it when a knowledge base has to be fed on a regular basis without redoing everything by hand.

terms.title: Response groundedness
terms.summary: Response groundedness measures whether an answer is genuinely backed by the context it was given.
terms.where: You see it in RAG evaluations, anti-hallucination tests, and quality dashboards for document assistants.

terms.title: Noise sensitivity
terms.summary: Noise sensitivity measures whether a RAG stays reliable when the context contains useless or misleading passages.
terms.where: You run into it in Ragas, robustness tests, and assistants that have to hold up against imperfect documents.

terms.title: Sonar Perplexity
terms.summary: Sonar is Perplexity's family of models built to search, source, and synthesize the web.
terms.where: You see it in the Perplexity API, monitoring agents, sourced research, and workflows that want answers with citations.

terms.title: Vercel AI SDK
terms.summary: The Vercel AI SDK helps you build AI interfaces, model calls, and agents inside web apps.
terms.where: You'll run into it in Next.js projects, chatbots, generative apps, response streaming, and multi-provider integrations.

terms.title: Hugging Face Hub
terms.summary: The Hugging Face Hub is the platform where models, datasets, Spaces, and AI-related files get published.
terms.where: You see it when you're looking for an open model, a demo, a dataset, or a model card.

terms.title: Messages API
terms.summary: The Messages API is Anthropic's entry point for sending a conversation to Claude and getting an answer back.
terms.where: You'll see it in Claude integrations, agents, API calls, streaming, and any tool that uses Anthropic.

terms.title: API endpoint
terms.summary: An API endpoint is the exact address a tool calls to request an action or fetch some data.
terms.where: You run into it in the OpenAI, Anthropic, Supabase, and Vercel docs, in webhooks, and in no-code integrations.

terms.title: Rate limit
terms.summary: A rate limit caps the number of requests or tokens an API accepts over a given period.
terms.where: You run into it when an automation runs too fast, when a provider returns a quota error, or when an agent fires off too many calls.

terms.title: Reasoning tokens
terms.summary: Reasoning tokens are the ones some models burn while thinking before they produce the visible answer.
terms.where: You run into them in reasoning models, API bills, effort settings, and cost/quality comparisons.

terms.title: Model card
terms.summary: A model card sums up a model's capabilities, limits, intended uses, and known risks.
terms.where: You'll see it on Hugging Face, in provider docs, and in serious AI model comparisons.

terms.title: Data retention
terms.summary: Data retention tells you how long a provider keeps your prompts, files, logs, or outputs.
terms.where: You run into it in API terms, enterprise plans, privacy policies, and AI tool audits.

terms.title: Speaker diarization
terms.summary: Speaker diarization splits a transcript by who is speaking.
terms.where: You see it in meeting notes, podcasts, customer calls, interviews, and advanced transcription tools.

terms.title: Voice activity detection
terms.summary: Voice activity detection spots when a person starts or stops talking.
terms.where: You run into it in voice agents, the Realtime API, phone assistants, and low-latency audio interfaces.

terms.title: Speech-to-speech
terms.summary: Speech-to-speech turns spoken input into spoken output, sometimes with a different voice or a different language.
terms.where: You see it in voice agents, AI dubbing, spoken translation, voice changers, and real-time assistants.

terms.title: Voice cloning
terms.summary: Voice cloning recreates a voice from audio samples.
terms.where: You run into it in dubbing tools, podcasts, avatars, deepfakes, and voice consent policies.

terms.title: Text to image
terms.summary: Text to image generates an image from a written prompt.
terms.where: You see it in Midjourney, GPT Image, DALL-E, Flux, Stable Diffusion, and visual creation tools.

terms.title: Inpainting
terms.summary: Inpainting replaces or fixes a specific area of an image with an AI generation.
terms.where: You see it when you remove an object, change a detail, repair a photo, or edit a masked area.

terms.title: Multimodal embedding
terms.summary: A multimodal embedding represents text, image, audio, or video in one and the same vector space.
terms.where: You'll run into it in text-to-image search, product catalogs, multimodal RAG, and engines that mix several formats.

terms.title: Video generation
terms.summary: Video generation creates or extends a video clip with a generative model.
terms.where: You see it in Sora, Veo, Runway, Pika, generated ads, social videos, and creative prototypes.

terms.title: Document Intelligence
terms.summary: Document Intelligence analyzes a document's text, layout, tables, fields, and structure.
terms.where: You run into it in Azure Document Intelligence, Google Document AI, Mistral OCR, invoice extraction, and document RAG.

terms.title: Deepfake
terms.summary: A deepfake is synthetic content that imitates a real person, often in image, voice, or video.
terms.where: You'll see it in debates about voice cloning, avatars, fraud, digital identity, and content verification.

terms.title: Browserbase
terms.summary: Browserbase provides cloud browsers to run web agents, tests, and automations.
terms.where: You run into it in browser agents, controlled scraping, cloud Playwright tests, and robust web automations.

terms.title: Browser Use
terms.summary: Browser Use is a framework and cloud for getting an AI agent to carry out web tasks.
terms.where: You'll see it in automations that fill out forms, navigate sites, or read pages like a real user.

terms.title: Stagehand
terms.summary: Stagehand combines Playwright with AI instructions to automate the web with more flexible actions.
terms.where: You'll run into it in web agents that can click, read, extract, and adapt when an interface changes.

terms.title: Headless browser
terms.summary: A headless browser is a browser with no visible window, driven by code or by an agent.
terms.where: You run into it in Playwright, Puppeteer, Browserbase, automated tests, scraping, and agents that browse the web.

terms.title: Cursor Rules
terms.summary: Cursor Rules are persistent instructions that frame how Cursor behaves in a project.
terms.where: You run into them in Cursor projects, coding conventions, team rules, and configs much like AGENTS.md.

terms.title: v0
terms.summary: v0 is Vercel's tool for generating interfaces, apps, and prototypes from instructions.
terms.where: You run into it in prompt-to-app workflows, quick mockups, React components, and projects tied to Vercel.

terms.title: Lovable
terms.summary: Lovable is an AI platform that generates and deploys web apps from plain-language requests.
terms.where: You run into it in AI no-code builders, SaaS prototypes, Supabase integrations, and app-building workflows that don't start from an empty repo.

terms.title: Supabase Realtime
terms.summary: Supabase Realtime pushes changes or messages live to connected users.
terms.where: You see it in chats, live dashboards, collaborative apps, notifications, and generated tools that need to react without a page reload.

terms.title: n8n expression
terms.summary: An n8n expression drops a dynamic value or a formula into a workflow field.
terms.where: You'll see it when a workflow needs to reuse an email, a date, an ID, or a piece of data from an earlier node.

terms.title: n8n error workflow
terms.summary: An n8n error workflow fires when an automation fails.
terms.where: You'll run into it to alert, log, retry, or safeguard a workflow that runs unattended.

terms.title: Deployment Protection (Vercel)
terms.summary: Vercel Deployment Protection controls who can access a preview or production deployment.
terms.where: You see it when an internal app, a prototype, or a preview shouldn't be publicly visible.

terms.title: Cowork (Claude)
terms.summary: Cowork is Claude working on your computer. You give it a folder, and it reads, sorts and creates files inside it.
terms.where: In the Claude desktop app, on Mac and Windows, with a paid plan (Pro or higher).
terms.example: You give Claude your Downloads folder and write "sort all of this by type and date". It creates the subfolders and moves the files into them.
terms.why: It is the simplest way to put AI to work on your real files, with no terminal and no code.
mistakes: Giving it your whole drive instead of a single folder.
Closing the app while it works on your files, which stops the task.
Handing it important files with no backup copy.

terms.title: ChatGPT Work
terms.summary: Work is the ChatGPT mode that completes a whole task, in several steps, and hands back a document, a spreadsheet, a deck or a site.
terms.where: In ChatGPT on the web, on your phone and in the desktop app (Mac and Windows), with a paid plan.
terms.example: You switch to Work and write "from these three quotes, build me a comparison table and tell me which one to pick". It hands back the table, ready to open.
terms.why: You go from answers you copy and paste to finished documents.
mistakes: Using Work for a quick question, when Chat answers faster.
Giving it your files without checking what it does with them.
Assuming the result is right because it looks polished.

terms.title: Agent mode
terms.summary: Agent mode is when AI stops just answering and chains several actions on its own to reach a goal.
terms.where: In Cowork on Claude, Work on ChatGPT, AI browsers like Comet or Atlas, and automation tools.
terms.example: You ask "find me three trains to Lyon on Friday morning". In agent mode, the AI opens the site, compares the times and suggests the three, instead of giving you tips on how to search.
terms.why: It is what saves the most time, and what needs the most attention.
mistakes: Letting it pay or send a message without checking.
Giving it a vague instruction, so it heads the wrong way.
Thinking an agent never makes mistakes because it sounds confident.

terms.title: Project (Claude, ChatGPT)
terms.summary: A project groups conversations, files and instructions on one topic, so the AI keeps the context from one time to the next.
terms.where: In Claude and in ChatGPT, on the web, on your phone and in the desktop app.
terms.example: You create a "My business" project, add your brochure and price list, and write one instruction: "always answer in a warm, friendly tone". Every new conversation starts from there.
terms.why: More accurate answers, without pasting your context every time.
mistakes: Putting everything in one catch-all project.
Uploading confidential documents without checking the privacy settings.
Forgetting to update the files when your prices change.

terms.title: AI browser
terms.summary: An AI browser is a web browser with built-in AI that reads the page with you and can act on it when you ask.
terms.where: Perplexity's Comet, OpenAI's Atlas, Chrome's AI features and the browser built into the Claude desktop app.
terms.example: On a product page, you ask "compare with the two other tabs and tell me the cheapest one delivered before Saturday". It reads the three pages and answers.
terms.why: The AI sees what you see, so you stop copying and pasting pages.
mistakes: Letting it sign in to your accounts without watching.
Thinking a malicious page cannot trick it.
Using it to buy something without checking the cart.
